items.title: 27.5.3 The Genetic Code and Protein Synthesis

source_refs.note: Topic 27.5.3 as printed (PDF 174): the book's paragraph, Figure 27.17 (redrawn) and Quick Check 27.4 (questions only).

blocks.text: Protein synthesis is a complex process involved in transferring genetic information encoded in the DNA. Two processes, transcription and translation are required for transmitting genetic information for the synthesis of numerous proteins in living organisms. The process starts with replication, i.e. making copies of DNA in the nucleus, the genetic instructions for making a protein are copied from a DNA gene into mRNA; this process is called transcription. When the mRNA strand is complete, it detaches from DNA and enters the cytoplasm, where it attaches to ribosomes. At the ribosomes, the code carried by mRNA is read and converted into a specific sequence of amino acids, forming a protein through the process called translation. Amino acids are arranged according to the sequence of bases in the RNA. The tRNA molecules release their amino acids, which join together in a chain, forming a polypeptide chain. The polypeptide chain grows as bonds form between the amino acids, and finally the complete protein molecule is formed.
book_errors: The process starts with replication, i.e. making copies of DNA in the nucleus

blocks.alt: From top to bottom: a looping arrow from DNA back to DNA labelled replication (DNA to DNA), DNA polymerase; DNA (a double strand); an arrow labelled transcription (DNA to RNA), RNA polymerase; RNA (a single strand); an arrow labelled translation (RNA to protein), ribosome; and a protein drawn as a chain of beads.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: Replication (DNA → DNA copying before cell division) is not a step of protein synthesis. Protein synthesis starts with transcription: in the nucleus, the genetic instructions for a protein are copied from a DNA gene into mRNA; translation follows at the ribosomes.

blocks.prompt:
a) Compare the stability provided by the sugar-phosphate backbone versus the inter-chain base pairing. In your answer, refer to the specific types of bonds and the number of bonds formed between:
• Adenine (A) and Thymine (T)
• Guanine (G) and Cytosine (C)
blocks.explanation: The backbone is held by strong covalent phosphodiester bonds, so each strand is very strong. The two strands are held together only by hydrogen bonds between the bases: two in an A–T pair and three in a G–C pair. Each hydrogen bond is weak, so the strands can separate for replication, but millions of them together hold the double helix firmly; a region with more G–C pairs is more stable.

blocks.prompt: b) How the DNA and RNA are chemically different? What are the similarities between these two?
blocks.explanation: Differences: DNA contains the sugar deoxyribose and the base thymine and is double-stranded; RNA contains ribose and uracil and is usually single-stranded. Similarities: both are polymers of nucleotides (phosphate, a five-carbon sugar and a base) joined by phosphodiester links, and both contain the bases A, G and C.

rows: Similarity: a polymer of nucleotides with phosphodiester links
Similarity: a polymer of nucleotides with phosphodiester links

blocks.prompt: c) Nearly every cell in the human body contains the exact same 23 pairs of chromosomes, yet a red blood cell produces haemoglobin while a skin cell produces keratin. Explain why.
blocks.explanation: Each type of cell switches on different genes: a developing red blood cell transcribes the gene for haemoglobin and a skin cell the gene for keratin, while the other genes stay switched off.
